disciplines.label: Financial
disciplines.pain: The EBITDA in the information memorandum has already been normalised by the seller, and working capital leaks in places the summary never mentions.
disciplines.result: Which adjustments hold, which don’t, and what cost base is left standing after closing.

disciplines.label: Commercial
disciplines.pain: Customer concentration and churn rarely make the summary page.
disciplines.result: Which customers carry the revenue, what the pricing will actually bear, and how much retention sits underneath the growth.

disciplines.label: Legal
disciplines.pain: The clauses that reach the margin sit in the schedules nobody reads to the end.
disciplines.result: Every clause that triggers on the transaction or on the margin, with clause number and page, and what of it can be renegotiated.

disciplines.label: Tax
disciplines.pain: A deferred position announces itself years after closing.
disciplines.result: Where the structure carries risk, and what belongs in the purchase agreement because of it.

disciplines.label: HR
disciplines.pain: Key people leave after closing, and the earn-out was resting on them.
disciplines.result: Who is contractually tied in, who isn’t, and what pension and collective labour agreements really cost.

disciplines.label: IT & technology
disciplines.pain: Technical debt is on nobody’s balance sheet, and licences run on inside contracts nobody has counted.
disciplines.result: What actually runs, what it costs to fix, and which licences consolidate after closing.

disciplines.label: AI
disciplines.pain: “AI-driven” is usually a licence on someone else’s model, and who owns the data goes unanswered.
disciplines.result: Whose model and whose data, what falls under the AI Act, and which processes genuinely automate.

disciplines.label: ESG
disciplines.pain: Reporting obligations move to the buyer along with the company.
disciplines.result: What has to be reported from here, and what that takes in investment.

disciplines.label: Operational
disciplines.pain: Lead times and single points of failure appear on no overview.
disciplines.result: Where the margin goes, which link carries the work on its own, and what automating those processes returns.

disciplines.label: Valuation & deal economics
disciplines.pain: The bid comes out of a model that hadn’t seen the findings yet.
disciplines.result: What the findings do to the price, and what room that leaves at the negotiating table.

pipeline.title: From upload to a finished finding
pipeline.lead: Five stages. The same five, every time, whether or not anyone is watching.

stages.title: Grounded retrieval
stages.body: The module goes into the data room and pulls the passages that answer its question.
stages.note: Confidential financial and personal data is pseudonymized before it reaches this layer.

stages.title: Drafting against the schema
stages.body: A claim without a document and a passage behind it is not a finding.

stages.title: Generate-critique-retry
stages.body: A reviewer agent critiques the draft and sends it back. Up to two retries per specialist.

stages.title: Four-layer grounding check
stages.body: Index, quote, entailment, second opinion. Each layer catches what the one before it missed.

stages.title: Cross-discipline reconciliation
stages.body: Findings are read against each other and resolved into one narrative.

stages.title: Human review and approval
stages.body: A named person reviews the findings before release.
stages.note: Pseudonymization is reversed only here, in the final delivered output.

grounding.title: Four checks, each narrower than the last
grounding.lead: A claim has to survive all four. One failure sends it back.

layers.title: Citation calibration
layers.body: Every citation index is checked against the set of passages that were actually retrieved.
layers.catches: Citations pointing at a document the run never opened.

layers.title: Lexical quote check
layers.body: The quoted text has to appear in the cited passage, character for character.
layers.catches: Paraphrase presented as a verbatim excerpt.

layers.title: Entailment judge
layers.body: A separate model reads the claim and the passage and rules on whether one follows from the other.
layers.catches: Real quotes that do not support the claim built on them.

layers.title: Second-opinion verify
layers.body: A local natural-language-inference model re-runs the judgment. This layer fails closed.
layers.catches: Whatever the first three let through.

grounding.repair: Claims that fail get one repair attempt: re-quote from source, then re-judge. Claims that still fail are cut or marked unconfirmed.

blocks.title: {blocks} conditions that stop auto-approval
blocks.lead: Retries are capped at two per specialist. These conditions end the loop regardless and route the draft to a person.

limits.title: What we don’t claim about the platform
limits.lead: Everything above describes a mechanism. None of it is a certified metric.
items: No audited accuracy rate. Internal benchmarks are single-dataset and unaudited.
No claim that the human gate is optional. It is mandatory.
No completed public case studies yet.
No uniform track record. The financial module has run end to end on a live deal and been verified against source documents. The reconciliation layer is younger.
No product-level technical due diligence. Source-code review, architecture assessment and scalability testing sit outside the standard pass.
No integrity or reputational screening. Background checks on people and counterparties run outside this platform.
No general availability. Factum is pre-launch.

items.q: Isn’t this just an AI chatbot with extra steps?
items.a: A chat session is one context window that you steer. This is {modules} pre-scoped modules in a fixed dependency order, with four grounding checks and a mandatory human gate. The difference is what happens when nobody is watching.

items.q: Why waves instead of running everything at once?
items.a: Tax cannot reason without the financial and legal reads. Valuation cannot price without tax. The dependency graph sets the order; wave 1 still runs eight modules in parallel.

items.q: What happens when the model doesn’t know?
items.a: It has to say so. A finding is either backed by a citation that survived four checks or flagged as unconfirmed. Fabricated sources are one of the {blocks} hard blocks.

items.q: How do I know the platform can carry findings this material?
items.a: The financial module is the most numerically exposed part of any read. It has run end to end on a live deal and been independently verified against source documents. Newer layers have less history, and we tell you which is which.

items.q: How fast is it?
items.a: The pipeline pass runs in hours. The finished, reviewed output takes days. We don’t quote a delivery date before seeing the data room.

cta.title: See it run on a real dispatch graph
cta.body: We open the dispatch graph, run a module, and follow one finding back to its source passage.
cta.note: Thirty minutes: a walkthrough of the platform, then your own situation.

gaps.title: What your data room is missing
gaps.lead: A buyer’s first move is to ask for what is not there. You get that list first, by name.
items: The documents a buyer will ask for and your room does not contain.
The years that are incomplete in an export, where a gap reads as something worse than it is.
The contracts referenced inside other contracts and never uploaded.
The gaps you already know about, so you can decide how to present them rather than be asked.
gaps.note: We can see that something is absent. Whether it was left out on purpose is not ours to say, and we do not say it.

boundaries.title: What a pre-sale sprint is not
boundaries.lead: The honest version, so it is not a conversation later.
items: Not a vendor due diligence opinion. That is a signed attest engagement and this is not one.
Not a guarantee of price. We can tell you what a buyer will find; what he does with it is his.
Not a fairness opinion, and not a valuation that stands on its own in front of a bank.
Not a clean-up service. We name what is missing; obtaining it is yours or your adviser’s.
Not walled off from your own adviser by default. If you want it kept separate, say so before we start.

items.q: How long before the process should we run this?
items.a: Early enough that the answer to a finding can still be “we fixed it”. Once the data room is live, the honest framing becomes “we know, and here is the context”. Both work. The first one is worth more.

items.q: Will the buyer know we did this?
items.a: Only if you tell them. Some sellers do, because arriving with your own findings and their context is a strong position. That is your call, not ours.

items.q: What if we find something serious?
items.a: Then you found it, months before somebody with an incentive to use it did. That is the reason to run it, not a reason not to.

items.q: Is this the same product as the buy-side sprint?
items.a: The same engine, the same dimensions and the same output contract. What differs is the question we point it at and the list you get at the end.

legal.title: Why this is not a chat window
legal.lead: One from the courts. One from your own NDA. One from the statute book.

items.title: A public AI tool is not a private one
items.body: In United States v. Heppner a federal court held that a defendant’s exchanges with a public AI assistant were neither privileged nor work product, and handed them to prosecutors. Where the work runs decides who can read it later.

items.title: Your NDA may not cover the tool
items.body: Most M&A NDAs permit disclosure only to named Representatives: staff, advisers, financing sources. An AI platform is rarely one of them. Putting the data room into a consumer tool can be the breach itself.

items.title: The EU AI Act runs on a clock
items.body: General-purpose AI obligations have applied since 2 August 2025. The Article 50 transparency duties follow on 2 August 2026. A documented human gate is easier to place inside that regime than a chat session nobody logged.

legal.note: None of this is legal advice. All three are reasons the pipeline is shaped the way it is.

items.title: What we keep, and why

header.title: The method, end to end
header.lead: The long version. What runs in which order, the contract every finding has to satisfy, and what a person checks before anything reaches you.

waves.title: {modules} modules, {waves} waves, one order
waves.lead: Nothing runs early. A module starts when the work it depends on is finished, which is why the run has a shape rather than a queue.

steps.title: Wave one — the independent reads
steps.body: {w1} modules open at the same moment. Financial, commercial, HR, IT, AI, ESG and operational go into the data room in parallel, alongside the information-memorandum screener and the monitoring set-up. None of them needs another module’s answer to start.

steps.title: Wave two — the reads that have to wait
steps.body: Tax and legal. Both reason about consequences: a tax position is a consequence of the structure the financial read has just described, and a legal exposure is usually a consequence of a commercial term. Running them first produces confident answers to the wrong question.

steps.title: Wave three — synthesis
steps.body: {w3} modules read across everything above them. Valuation recalculates the price through the findings rather than around them. Deal economics, portfolio and post-merger integration take the same body of findings and ask a different question of it.

steps.title: Wave four — the documents
steps.body: {w4} deliverables, assembled from the waves above: vendor due diligence, the investment-committee memo, the teaser or CIM, the financing memorandum, and the document factory for whatever else the process needs.

steps.title: Wave five — after the deal
steps.body: {w5} modules on their own clock: exit readiness and portfolio health. They are not part of the sprint and do not wait for it.

steps.title: Wave six — the periodic report
steps.body: The investment-committee report sits alone in the last wave, because modules inside one wave run at the same time. Next to exit readiness and portfolio health it would read the previous round’s chapters, or nothing at all on a first run.

waves.note: Waves one and two are the diligence pass. Everything after them is what you do with it.

contract.title: The output contract, field by field
contract.lead: Five fields. A finding that cannot fill all five is not delivered as a finding.

items.title: Module
items.body: Which of the {modules} produced it. Pre-scoped, so the question was written before the data room was opened rather than improvised from what happened to be in it.
items.fail: There is no free-text lane. No module, no finding.

items.title: Finding
items.body: One claim, in one sentence. Compound claims are split, because a sentence with two claims in it can only ever be half-checked.
items.fail: Too vague to check is treated the same as wrong.

items.title: Verbatim excerpt
items.body: The supporting passage, quoted word for word. Not summarised, not tidied, not shortened to fit.
items.fail: A paraphrase presented as a quote fails the lexical check and goes back.

items.title: Source document and passage
items.body: File name and page, so you can open it yourself. This is the field that makes a finding arguable instead of authoritative.
items.fail: A citation that does not resolve to a real passage is a hard block, not a warning.

items.title: Human review
items.body: The person who approved it, by name, before release. Every finding, every mandate.
items.fail: There is no fast lane for a busy week.

contract.note: A claim that fails a check gets one repair attempt: re-quote from source, then re-judge. What still fails is either cut or delivered marked unconfirmed. Unconfirmed is a legitimate output. A quietly dropped claim is not.

trail.title: What gets recorded, and in what order
trail.lead: A finding is a chain. Every link is written down, which is the only reason a question three months from now has an answer.
steps: The document enters the room and is indexed. Confidential financial and personal values are pseudonymised before any model sees them.
The module retrieves the passages that answer its own question, and only those.
The draft is written against the contract above. A claim with no passage behind it does not get written.
A reviewing pass critiques the draft and sends it back. Two retries, then the loop stops and a person takes it.
Four grounding checks run in sequence: the citation index, the quote itself, whether the claim follows from the passage, and a second opinion that fails closed.
A named person reviews, reconciles and approves. Pseudonymised values are reversed here and nowhere earlier.
You receive the finding with its document reference attached, and it stays openable afterwards.
trail.note: The worked example — a clause on page 14 of a fictional master services agreement, and the finding it produced — is on the homepage.

gate.title: What the reviewer actually does
gate.lead: “Human in the loop” is a phrase. This is the sequence behind it.
items: Opens the cited document and reads the passage against the claim built on it.
Decides materiality — which findings change what you pay, or whether you sign at all.
Resolves conflicts between modules. Two disciplines reading one fact differently is itself a finding, not an error to smooth over.
Marks what could not be confirmed, and says why.
Reverses the pseudonymisation in the final output, and only there.
Signs. One named person, accountable for the document you receive.
gate.note: {blocks} failure classes end the automated loop early and route the draft to that person regardless of how it scored.

stops.title: Where the method stops
stops.lead: Everything above is work a machine can be held to. A good part of diligence is not, and pretending otherwise is how these systems lose the room.
stops.link: What AI cannot do in due diligence

header.title: What AI cannot do in due diligence
header.lead: We sell an AI pipeline. This page is about the part of the job it does not do, and who does that instead.

limits.title: Five things no model does on a data room
limits.lead: These are not tuning problems. They are categories of work that sit outside what a language model is.

items.title: Decide what matters
items.body: A model can find every change-of-control clause in the room. It cannot tell you which one kills the deal. Materiality is a judgement about your structure, your price and your appetite, and none of those is in the data room.
items.human: The reviewer ranks findings against the deal you are actually doing.

items.title: Cite the document that isn’t there
items.body: Retrieval reads what was uploaded. The most expensive thing in diligence is often an absence — the contract nobody filed, the year missing from the payroll export. An absence has no passage to quote, so no grounded system can raise it as a finding.
items.human: The data-gap tracker is a person’s running list of what was asked for and never arrived. It is delivered alongside the findings.

items.title: Read what nobody wrote down
items.body: Management sessions, the site visit, a customer reference call, an integrity check on a shareholder. These produce the findings that move bids most often, and none of them starts as a document.
items.human: Your own team, or your advisers. This platform does not do it and does not imply otherwise.

items.title: Tell soft from hidden
items.body: A number can be weak because the business is weak, or because the seller shaped the process. On the page the two look identical. Telling them apart takes knowledge of how sellers behave, not of what the file says.
items.human: Someone who has run the other side of the table. On our side that is a leveraged-finance banker.

items.title: Be accountable
items.body: A model cannot be a Representative under your NDA, cannot answer to your investment committee, and cannot sign. Accountability is not a capability you add to a system. It attaches to a person or it does not exist.
items.human: One named person approves every output and stands behind it.

limits.note: If a vendor claims their system does any of the five, ask which page it cited.

gate.title: Which is why the gate is mandatory
gate.lead: The human step is not a safety blanket bolted onto a finished product. It is where four of the five above actually get done.
items: A name and a date on every output, not a confidence score.
Materiality decided against your deal, not against a benchmark.
Unconfirmed claims marked unconfirmed rather than quietly dropped.
One person to argue with when you disagree.

machine.title: And what the machine is genuinely better at
machine.lead: The honest version of this argument runs both ways.

items.title: It reads all of it
items.body: A team under deadline reads a sample and calls it coverage. Page 900 gets the same attention as page 9.

items.title: It does not get tired
items.body: The same schema, the same checks and the same standard of evidence at the end of the run as at the start. Consistency is what people are worst at and machines are free at.

items.title: It runs in parallel
items.body: {first} modules opening at once instead of queueing behind each other is where the days come from — not from any single answer arriving faster.

ask.title: Three questions for any AI diligence vendor
ask.lead: Including us. The answers tell you more than the demo does.

items.title: Who signs?
items.body: If the answer is a dashboard, nobody does. Ask for a name, and ask what happens when that name is wrong.

items.title: What happens to a claim that can’t be cited?
items.body: There are three honest answers: it is cut, it is flagged, or it is shown with its evidence gap visible. A system with no answer is showing you unmarked guesses.

items.title: What does it do when a document is missing?
items.body: Silence is the wrong answer. A missing document should produce an item on a list, not the absence of a finding.

boundaries.title: What a partnership does not include
boundaries.lead: Some are commitments to existing partners. The rest is the honest state of a pre-launch company.
items: No white-labelled claim of certification or audit. We can’t stand behind a badge we don’t hold.

header.title: What this site collects, and what an engagement does
header.lead: This page covers the website. Engagement data handling is governed by the agreement we sign.

sections.title: This website
body: No contact form, no account system, no login. There is nothing here to submit.
Your language comes from the URL you are on. No cookie, no IP-based detection.
Visits are counted with Plausible Analytics: no cookie, no fingerprint, no cross-site profile, data held in the EU. It records the page, the referring site, the country and the device type.
That count writes nothing to your device. That is why this site carries no cookie banner.

sections.title: Booking a demo
body: The booking link takes you to Cal.com, a third-party scheduling service. What you enter there is processed under their terms and shared with us so we can hold the meeting.
We use it to prepare for the demo and to follow up. We do not add it to a marketing list.

sections.title: Documents you share with us
body: No documents are shared through this website. Access is agreed separately, in writing.

During an engagement, confidential data is pseudonymized before analysis and reversed only in the final output. Analysis runs on Google Vertex AI in an EU region under a Data Processing Agreement. The model provider does not keep your documents or train on them.
Retention and deletion terms on our own side are set in the engagement agreement.

sections.title: Your rights
body: Under the GDPR you can ask what personal data we hold, have it corrected or deleted, or object to how it is used. Raise it in the demo or reply to any email from us.
If you are not satisfied, you can complain to the Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens, the Dutch data protection authority.
